opus-5.5.text:
I think academia should focus on questions that industry labs aren't well positioned to answer, because we can't compete on scale. Training the biggest single model isn't our comparative advantage. Multi-agent problems, though, are full of questions that are conceptually hard rather than compute-hard.

The first area I care about is cooperation with unknown partners. Most multi-agent RL work trains agents that cooperate very well with copies of themselves. In self-play they coordinate perfectly. Put them next to a human, or an agent trained with a different random seed, and they often fall apart, because they've learned private conventions. So how do you build an agent that can work with someone it has never seen before? That's the zero-shot coordination or ad hoc teamwork problem. I think it's fundamental, and you can study it with modest compute in carefully designed environments.

The second area is diversity. In a game with many equilibria, standard training converges to one solution, often a fairly arbitrary one. We've done some work on deliberately discovering diverse strategies, so you get a population of meaningfully different behaviors instead of one. That matters for robustness, for training partners, and honestly for understanding the structure of the game itself. It's an algorithmic question, and academia can make real progress there.

The third area is becoming more urgent with LLMs. Now that we have language agents, the multi-agent question changes shape. It's no longer only about Atari-style games or StarCraft. It's about multiple LLM agents negotiating, collaborating on software, or deceiving each other in social deduction games like Werewolf. How do you get agents to reason strategically, model what others believe, and communicate honestly instead of just generating plausible text? Current models are surprisingly weak at genuine strategic reasoning. Combining RL with language models to get real strategic behavior is wide open.

Fourth, and related, is evaluation. In single-agent settings you have a benchmark and a score. In multi-agent settings your performance depends on who you're playing with, so "how good is this agent" is a genuinely subtle question. Academia should help define good evaluation protocols, because otherwise everyone just reports numbers against baselines they chose themselves.

Last, I'd encourage people to think about human–AI interaction as a multi-agent problem. Once AI systems are deployed, the human is another agent with their own goals and adaptations. Alignment is, in a sense, a multi-agent problem too. So I'd say the questions worth pursuing are generalization to new partners, diversity, strategic reasoning in language agents, and evaluation. They're less about scale and more about finding the right formulation, which is where universities can really contribute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses several multi-agent research areas and says these questions matter beyond single-agent benchmarks, but it does not prioritize interaction models for a world where everyone uses agents over solving a benchmark task.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss human feedback or compare its richness with examples of successful and incorrect behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I've spent time on both sides, at OpenAI and now in academia at Tsinghua, and the honest answer is that academia should not try to compete with industry on scale. If your research question is "what happens when we throw ten thousand GPUs at a multi-agent system," you've already lost. Industry will do that better, faster, and they'll do it without publishing.

So the questions I find interesting for academia are the ones where scale isn't the bottleneck, where the bottleneck is understanding.

The first one is: when do multiple agents actually help? We all have this intuition that collaboration is powerful, we have the hide-and-seek results, we have debate, we have all these demos. But if you look carefully, in a lot of cases a single stronger model does just as well. So the scientific question is, what's the structure of a problem that genuinely requires decomposition across agents? Is it about information asymmetry? Is it about the depth of search? Is it just a compute-splitting trick? I don't think we have a clean theory, and that's exactly the kind of thing a PhD student can spend three years on without needing a giant cluster.

The second one is communication and emergence. In the old multi-agent reinforcement learning days we spent a lot of effort on emergent communication protocols, and now with language models the agents already speak English, so people think the problem is solved. I actually think it's harder now. When two LLM agents talk to each other, are they really exchanging information, or are they just producing text that looks like coordination? How do you measure that? How do you tell the difference between agents that have a shared plan and agents that are each hallucinating a shared plan? That's a measurement problem, a benchmark problem, and benchmarks are something academia has historically done very well.

The third thing, which I care about more and more, is the game-theoretic side. Once you have many agents that are deployed by different people with different objectives, you're no longer doing cooperative learning, you're doing mechanism design. How do these systems behave when they negotiate, when they can deceive, when the incentives aren't aligned? Industry mostly builds single-company agent systems where everyone cooperates by construction. The messy, mixed-motive, multi-principal setting is wide open, and it's also where a lot of the safety questions live.

And then there's a more practical one, which is training. Right now most of the multi-agent LLM work is prompting. You take a frozen model, write a role for it, connect a few copies. Very little of it is actually learning in the multi-agent loop. The reason is that multi-agent RL with language models is extremely unstable, the credit assignment is terrible, and nobody has good open infrastructure for it. I think academia should build that infrastructure and own that problem, the way the community once owned things like PPO and the early MARL algorithms. Small models, clean environments, real learning, open code. If you can get two 7B models to genuinely improve each other through interaction, that's a much more important result than one more impressive demo with GPT.

So if I summarize: ask why, not how big. Build the measurements. Study the adversarial and mixed-motive cases. And make the training actually work in the open. Those are the places where a university lab has a real advantage rather than a disadvantage.

r002.rationale: The response discusses training and evaluation, but does not say that human feedback can be richer than examples of successful and incorrect behavior.

r003.rationale: The response recommends several open research directions, but does not recommend pursuing questions whose importance may emerge two or three years later.

astra-6.text:
I think academia should focus on the fundamental questions that become important when you have many agents learning and acting together. How do they learn to cooperate? When is communication useful, and what do they need to communicate? How do you get an agent to work with a partner it has never encountered during training?

That last question is particularly interesting. If you train a group of agents together, they might develop a very effective strategy, but it could depend on conventions that only that group understands. Working with a new agent—or with a human—requires something more flexible. We need to understand what makes that kind of generalization possible.

There are also questions about mixed incentives. Agents may share some goals and disagree on others. Can they coordinate without becoming vulnerable to exploitation? What happens as the number of agents grows?

For academia, I think the opportunity is to create clear experimental settings where we can isolate these problems and understand why a method works. A useful contribution could be a small experiment that exposes a fundamental limitation, rather than simply a larger system with a better score.

sol-6.1.text:
I think academia should focus on the fundamental questions that become important when you have many agents learning and acting together. How do they learn to cooperate? When do they need to communicate, and what information should they share? What happens when their goals are only partially aligned?

One particularly interesting question is whether an agent can cooperate with a partner it has never seen before. If you train a group of agents together, they can develop conventions that work within that group. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they can work with a new agent, or with a human. Understanding that gap is a good research direction.

We also need better ways to evaluate these systems. A higher team reward doesn’t tell us whether the agents have learned robust cooperation or found a very specific trick. Academia can contribute controlled experiments and clear problem formulations that help us understand why a method works, where it fails, and whether the behavior generalizes.
